summary: Lists the requirements that a callout protocol must meet to support remote execution of OPES services, where an edge device hands data to another server for processing. The requirements are meant to help evaluate candidate protocols and guide their design.

plainLanguage.summary: If one helper cannot do a job, they pass it to another helper in another room. This document lists what the passing method must be able to do.

questions: what is an opes callout protocol
subtitle: What a protocol must do when an OPES processor hands data to a remote callout server for processing.

tldr.problem: An OPES processor sometimes hands application messages to remote callout servers to run services, and a callout protocol is needed for that hand-off.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists functional, performance and security requirements for that callout protocol: reliable transport, transactions over connections, asynchronous exchange, fragmentation, keep-alives, negotiation, metadata, low latency and strong security.
tldr.outcome: It is a checklist for judging candidate protocols and guiding a new one; it defines no protocol itself.

today: RFC 3836 is an Informational RFC, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is the requirements companion to the architecture in RFC 3835.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The OPES architecture (RFC 3835) lets a data provider, a data consumer and zero or more OPES processors cooperate on application services that analyze, and possibly transform, application-level messages. Rules installed on the OPES processor govern execution. A triggered rule can run a service locally, or the processor can pass the work to one or more remote callout servers using a callout protocol.

This document states the requirements for that protocol, in three groups: functional, performance and security. Each requirement is a statement followed by brief explanation.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes the helper in the middle sends a job to a specialist elsewhere. This paper lists the rules for how that message must work.

sections.title: Functional Requirements: Transactions and Connections
sections.content:
The protocol MUST provide ordered reliability, and SHOULD also offer unordered reliability, ideally by being used over a transport such as TCP or SCTP. It MUST apply congestion avoidance matching RFC 2914.

A callout transaction is a callout request plus a callout response, each possibly several protocol messages. A request MUST carry a partial or complete application message; a response MUST report the result and MAY carry a modified message. Either side MUST be able to end a transaction early without losing application data, since a content analysis service may classify an object after only its first few bytes.

A callout connection is an application-layer logical connection carrying multiple transactions. It MUST always be started by the OPES processor, and either end MAY close it without disturbing ongoing transactions. Multiplexing several callout connections over one transport connection is allowed only with flow control that guarantees fairness.
sections.plainLanguage: The messenger must never lose your package, must be allowed to stop early if the answer is already clear, and the sender is always the one who starts the conversation.

sections.title: Asynchronous Exchange, Fragments and Keep-Alives
sections.content:
The protocol MUST support asynchronous exchange: several callout requests can be outstanding, and responses can be matched to requests. A callout server MUST be able to respond before it has received the whole request.

It MUST allow messages to be sent in smaller fragments in both directions, and the receiver must be able to reassemble them. This matters for very large messages, such as audio or video streams, or messages of unknown size, so the processor can start a transaction before the whole message has arrived.

It MUST provide a keep-alive mechanism so each end can detect the other's failure even when idle. Detecting a failed callout server may let the processor switch to a stand-by server. The protocol SHOULD also be NAT-friendly.
sections.plainLanguage: You should be able to send many notes without waiting for each answer, cut a long letter into pieces, and check every so often that the other helper is still there.

sections.title: Scale, Negotiation and Metadata
sections.content:
An OPES processor MUST be able to talk to several callout servers at once, and one callout server MUST be able to serve several processors. The protocol SHOULD be application protocol-agnostic but MUST at least be compatible with HTTP.

The endpoints MUST be able to negotiate capabilities and connection parameters in a deterministic process that ends in agreement or in a finding that they are incompatible. Examples include protocol version, fail-over behavior, heartbeat rate and security parameters. The transport protocol MUST NOT be chosen by negotiation. Connection parameters MUST be negotiated per connection, before any transactions.

Requests and responses MUST be able to carry metadata and instructions: the type or parts of the forwarded message, an ordered list of OPES services to apply, cacheability of responses, whether the processor kept a local copy, and information about service operations performed so that tracing requirements can be met.
sections.plainLanguage: Both helpers agree on the rules before they start, and each note can carry labels such as what is inside and what to do with it.

sections.title: Performance and Security Requirements
sections.content:
For performance, the protocol SHOULD have minimal latency, for example by keeping headers small and simple, because callout transactions add delay to the application transaction on the data path.

For security, endpoints MUST be able to authenticate each other with cryptographic methods, and the protocol MUST provide message authentication, confidentiality, integrity and mutual authentication, preferably by using existing security mechanisms or by referring to a lower-level security protocol. If hop-by-hop encryption is required on the content path, it MUST extend to the callout link, and a different encryption key MUST be used for each encrypted content stream. Encryption MAY be optional only when both ends sit in one administrative domain with strong confidentiality guarantees. Across untrusted domains, authentication and message protection MUST be used. Any communication carrying privacy-relevant information MUST be encrypted.

The RFC's Security Considerations section simply points to these requirements.
sections.plainLanguage: The messenger has to be quick, and the two helpers must prove who they are and keep notes secret from outsiders.
